This guideline, titled Counseling of Women to Improve Breastfeeding Practices, is the first evidence-informed guideline from WHO on this intervention. It complements other WHO interventions and guidance, such as breastfeeding counseling training courses, infant and young child feeding counseling, and tools for managing at-risk mothers and infants under six months of age. It also aligns with guidelines on optimal feeding of low birth-weight infants, protecting and promoting breastfeeding in maternity and newborn facilities, and infant feeding in emergencies. The guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the optimal timing, frequency, mode, and provider of breastfeeding counseling to improve breastfeeding practices. It is intended for policymakers, technical advisors, and program staff involved in designing and implementing breastfeeding counseling programs. The recommendations aim to improve the quality and delivery of services to pregnant women and mothers who wish to breastfeed, as well as to enhance monitoring of health system quality by defining expected services and staff competencies. The guideline emphasizes that breastfeeding counseling should be provided to all pregnant women and mothers with young children, both during the antenatal and postnatal periods, and up to 24 months or longer. Counseling should occur at least six times and additionally as needed. Face-to-face counseling is recommended, but remote modes such as telephone counseling may also be used in specific contexts. Counseling should be delivered as a continuum of care by appropriately trained healthcare professionals and community-based lay or peer breastfeeding counselors. Breastfeeding counseling should address challenges and contexts that may affect breastfeeding, such as low birth weight, disability, cesarean delivery, public breastfeeding, and humanitarian emergencies. It should empower women to breastfeed while respecting their personal situations and choices. Counseling is not intended to be a directive intervention but rather a supportive process that provides women with the skills, confidence, and information needed to make informed decisions about feeding their infants and children. The guideline also highlights the importance of breastfeeding counseling in emergency preparedness plans and responses for infant and young child feeding. It underscores that counseling should be sensitive, effective, and tailored to individual needs, helping mothers overcome barriers and make informed choices about feeding their children.
